query: How should we derive and operationalize r_e(L) — equity cost as a function of leverage — using CAPM, SVRM, implied equity volatility, or an endogenous limited-liability model, and which approach is most empirically tractable?

response.query: How should we derive and operationalize r_e(L) — equity cost as a function of leverage — using CAPM, SVRM, implied equity volatility, or an endogenous limited-liability model, and which approach is most empirically tractable?
response.answer: To derive r_e(L), use CAPM for a base cost of equity, then adjust for leverage using debt ratios. Market-implied cost of equity is often more empirically tractable. Limited-liability models are complex but can refine equity cost under leverage.

results.title: Musings on Markets: Alternatives to the CAPM: Part 4: Market-Implied cost of equity
results.content:
Title: Musings on Markets: Alternatives to the CAPM: Part 4: Market-Implied cost of equity
### Alternatives to the CAPM: Part 4: Market-Implied cost of equity. Using a very simple dividend discount model, you can back out the cost of equity for this company from the existing stock price:. Value of stock  = Dividends next year / (Cost of equity - growth rate). The mechanics of computing implied cost of equity become messier as you go from dividends to estimated cash flows and from stable growth models to high growth models, but the principle remains the same. 1. One is to use a conventional cost of equity in the valuation and to compare the market-implied cost of equity to the conventional one to see how much "margin for error" you have in your estimate. 2. The second is to compute a market-implied cost of equity for an entire sector sector and to use this cost as the cost of equity for all companies in that sector. Thus, I could compute the implied cost of equity for all banks of 9%, using an index of banking stocks and expected aggregate dividends on that index. 3. The third is to compute the market-implied cost of equity for the same company each period for a number of periods and to use that average as the cost of equity when valuing the company now. I use traditional models of risk and return to estimate costs of equity in valuation but I use market-implied costs of equity extensively. When I value individual companies, I do compare my estimates of cost of equity with the market-implied estimates. Finally, when I am concerned that the beta for a firm is not reflecting its underlying risk, because the sector itself has changed, I compute a market-implied cost of equity for the sector. Consequently, I used the S&P banking index to back out an implied cost of equity (which yielded an estimate almost 4% higher than the CAPM estimate) and used it in my valuations.
